unit.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Changes
unit.blurb: Reactions and processes that release heat or take it in: combustion, neutralisation, freezing and heat packs; decomposition, photosynthesis, melting and cold packs.

O1.t: Identify exothermic reactions from a temperature rise and give examples such as combustion, neutralisation and respiration.

O2.t: Describe exothermic processes such as freezing, dissolving and crystallisation, and their uses.

O3.t: Identify endothermic reactions from a temperature fall and give examples such as thermal decomposition and photosynthesis.

O4.t: Describe endothermic processes such as melting, evaporation and dissolving some salts, and measure temperature changes.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 7: Exothermic and Endothermic Changes.
Nearly three billion people don't have clean fuel for cooking.
Biogas digesters use bacteria to turn crop waste and animal manure into biogas,
a cleaner fuel. Some changes release energy, and some take it in.
Let's find out which is which.
When wood burns, it reacts with oxygen and releases its stored chemical energy as heat,
warming the air around it.
'Exo' means out, and 'thermic' means heat.
An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the temperature goes up.
The products end up with less energy than the reactants.
We can often notice the energy: a sparkler gives off heat and light.
And when plaster of Paris is mixed with water,
it reacts to form gypsum.
A setting plaster cast feels warm, because the reaction releases heat.
Water in a beaker is at 20 degrees Celsius.
A spoonful of solid calcium chloride is stirred in.
Predict: will the temperature go up, go down or stay the same?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The calcium chloride dissolves as it is stirred.
The thermometer rises to 38 degrees Celsius.
The beaker feels warm.
Explain what you saw.
Dissolving calcium chloride releases heat to the surroundings,
so the temperature of the water goes up.
A change that releases heat is exothermic.
This is how some self-heating packs and hand warmers work.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
There are many exothermic reactions.
Combustion is burning fuel in oxygen.
Neutralisation is an acid reacting with an alkali to make a salt and water.
Hydration is a substance reacting with water, like cement setting.
Reactive metals reacting with water, like sodium, are exothermic too.
Rusting releases heat slowly.
And aerobic respiration in your cells releases energy from glucose.
Remember, a reaction doesn't always make one pure product:
often it makes a mixture of substances.
An exothermic process is any change that releases heat, including physical changes.
When water freezes, its particles lose energy,
slow down and lock into fixed positions, releasing heat.
No new substance is formed, and the change can be reversed.
Dissolving some substances, like calcium chloride or solid sodium hydroxide, releases heat too,
so the solution feels warm.
Instant heat packs for sports injuries work this way.
Crystallisation, when crystals form from a supersaturated solution, is also exothermic.
Press a reusable hand warmer, and it crystallises,
heating up to about 54 degrees Celsius.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid, 5 cm³ at a time, to 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution in an insulated cup. Use the data to describe and explain how the temperature changes. Comment on how reliable the conclusion is.
adv.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: The temperature rises to a peak at 15 cm³
Quotes data with units, e.g. 21.0 °C to 30.1 °C
Neutralisation is exothermic, so it releases energy
After the peak the alkali is used up, and cooler acid / heat loss lowers the temperature
Only one trial: repeat to check the results are reliable

adv.model: As the acid is added the temperature rises from 21.0 °C to a peak of 30.1 °C at 15 cm³. The temperature rises because neutralisation is exothermic, so energy is released. After 15 cm³ all of the alkali has been used up, so no more energy is released. Adding more cooler acid and heat lost to the surroundings make the temperature fall to 27.6 °C. The results come from only one trial, so the experiment should be repeated to check they are reliable.

partial.text: The temperature goes up from 21.0 °C to 30.1 °C when the acid is added. This happens because the reaction between the acid and the alkali is exothermic. After that the temperature goes down again to 27.6 °C at the end. The cup is insulated so it keeps the energy in the mixture for longer.
partial.why: Data, rise and exothermic; no reason for the fall and no comment on reliability

partial.text: The temperature changes a lot when you add the acid to the alkali in the cup. It goes up and then it goes down again near the end of the experiment. The acid and the alkali react together and make a salt and water. The student used a polystyrene cup with a lid so that the test is fair.
partial.why: Only the rise and fall; no data and no energy idea

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A reusable hand warmer contains a solution of sodium ethanoate. When a metal disc inside is clicked, crystals form and the pack warms to 54 °C. Explain why the pack gets warm, and how it can be used again.
adv.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: Crystals form / the solution crystallises
Crystallisation is exothermic and releases energy
The energy is transferred to the hands / surroundings
To reuse it, heat it in hot water so the crystals dissolve again

adv.model: When the disc is clicked, the dissolved sodium ethanoate forms crystals. Crystallisation is an exothermic change, so it releases energy. This energy is transferred to your hands and the surroundings, so the pack feels warm. To reuse the pack, you put it in boiling water so the crystals dissolve again. This takes in energy, so the pack is ready to use next time.

partial.text: When you click the disc, the liquid inside the pack turns into crystals. This makes the pack hot, so your hands get warm. The pack stays warm for quite a long time in your pocket. You can use the same pack many times in winter.
partial.why: Crystals and energy to the hands; no exothermic idea and no way to reuse it

partial.text: The pack is exothermic because it gets hot when you click the metal disc. It is very useful in winter for keeping warm outside. People take them when they go skiing or walking. It is better than a battery warmer because it has no wires.
partial.why: Names exothermic but explains nothing else

ext.prompt: A student burns three fuels under a can holding 100 cm³ of water and records the temperature rise. She claims: “Paraffin releases the most energy per gram.” Evaluate her claim using the data, and suggest two improvements to the experiment.
ext.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: Works out wax per gram: 14 °C for 0.5 g ≈ 28 °C per gram
Paraffin gives the largest rise (31 °C), so the data support the claim
The difference from wax is small (about 3 °C), so the claim is uncertain
Energy is lost to the surroundings, so not all of it heats the water
Improvement: repeat each test and calculate an average
Improvement: burn the same mass, use a draught shield, lid or insulation

ext.model: The data support the claim because paraffin gave the largest temperature rise, 31 °C for 1.0 g. Wax gave 14 °C for 0.5 g, so per gram it would give about 28 °C, which is close to paraffin. The difference is only about 3 °C, so we cannot be sure the claim is correct from one trial. Some energy is also lost to the surroundings, so the water does not take in all of it. The student should repeat each test three times and calculate an average. She should also burn the same mass of each fuel and use a shield to stop draughts.

partial.text: Paraffin is the best fuel because it has the biggest temperature rise, which is 31 °C. Ethanol only made 24 °C and wax only made 14 °C, so wax is the worst fuel. I agree with the student that paraffin releases the most energy. She should repeat the experiment three times to make her results more reliable and fair.
partial.why: Supports the claim and suggests repeats, but misses the per-gram comparison, the small difference and heat loss

partial.text: Paraffin gives a rise of 31 °C and ethanol gives a rise of 24 °C for the same mass. Wax was only 0.5 g, so if we double it, wax would give about 28 °C per gram. This is very close to paraffin, so the claim might not be right. The student cannot be sure which fuel is really the best from these results.
partial.why: Good per-gram reasoning and the uncertainty, but no improvements and no energy-loss idea

ext.prompt: An iron hand warmer (iron + oxygen → iron oxide) reaches 60 °C in air. The same pack sealed in a bag of nitrogen stays at 20 °C. Opened in pure oxygen, it reaches 60 °C in half the time. What is the best conclusion?

options.t: The reaction needs oxygen, is exothermic, and goes faster when there is more oxygen.
options.fb: Yes – no oxygen, no temperature rise; more oxygen, faster rise.

options.t: Nitrogen is endothermic, so it takes in the energy from the iron.
options.fb: Nitrogen is just a gas that does not react with iron. The pack stays cold because there is no oxygen to react with.

options.t: Iron releases energy by itself; oxygen only makes the pack look different.
options.fb: In nitrogen there is no rise at all, so the iron cannot release the energy on its own.

options.t: Oxygen is the fuel that burns, and iron only stores the heat.
options.fb: Iron is the reactant that is oxidised. Oxygen is needed, but it is not a fuel.

ext.prompt: Dissolving 5 g of calcium chloride in 50 cm³ of water raises the temperature by 8 °C. The same 5 g is dissolved in 100 cm³ of water instead. Predict the temperature rise.
ext.hint: Same energy released, twice as much water to warm up.
ext.reason: The same amount of salt releases the same energy, but it is shared by twice as much water, so the rise is half: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 °C.

ext.prompt: On frosty nights, fruit farmers spray their trees with water. Ice forms on the buds, but the buds are not damaged. Explain how spraying water protects the buds.
ext.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: The water freezes into ice on the buds
Freezing is exothermic and releases energy
The energy stops the bud falling below 0 °C
Spraying continues all night, so freezing keeps releasing energy
The layer of ice insulates the bud from the colder air

ext.model: The sprayed water freezes into a layer of ice on the buds. Freezing is exothermic, so the water releases energy as it turns to ice. This energy stops the bud temperature from falling below 0 °C. The farmers keep spraying water all night, so freezing continues and keeps releasing energy. The ice layer also covers the buds and insulates them from the colder air.

partial.text: The water that the farmers spray turns to ice on the buds. The ice covers the buds and keeps them warm like a blanket. This stops the frost from getting to the buds. So the buds are not damaged and the fruit can still grow in the spring.
partial.why: Freezing and insulation, but no energy released and no link to 0 °C

partial.text: Freezing is an exothermic change, so it gives out energy. When the water freezes on the buds, this energy warms the buds a little. The buds are then protected from the frost at night. This is why the farmers spray the trees when it is very cold.
partial.why: The exothermic energy idea only; nothing about 0 °C, spraying all night or insulation

captions: Citric acid and baking soda, the ingredients of sherbet,
are added to water at 20 degrees Celsius.
Predict: what will happen to the temperature?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The mixture fizzes as carbon dioxide gas is made.
The thermometer falls to 14 degrees Celsius.
The beaker feels cold.
Explain what you saw.
This reaction takes in heat from its surroundings,
including the water and your hand, so the temperature falls.
A change that takes in heat is endothermic.
That is why sherbet feels cool and tingly on your tongue.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Some reactions take in heat.
'Endo' means in, so an endothermic reaction absorbs energy, usually heat,
from its surroundings. The temperature falls, and the mixture feels cold.
The products end up with more energy than the reactants.
Sherbet powder contains citric acid and baking soda.
Add water, and they react, fizzing and feeling cold: an endothermic reaction!
You might feel it on your tongue.
Baking bread is endothermic too: the dough absorbs heat from the oven,
and reactions change its sugars and proteins, giving bread its colour,
texture and flavour.
Thermal decomposition is endothermic: heat green copper carbonate,
and it breaks down into black copper oxide and carbon dioxide.
Photosynthesis is endothermic too:
plants take in light energy and store it as chemical energy in glucose.
Physical changes can be endothermic.
When ice melts, its particles take in heat,
vibrate faster and break free to flow.
When a liquid evaporates,
its particles gain enough energy to escape as a gas.
Dissolving some salts, like ammonium chloride, takes in heat,
so cold packs for injuries feel icy.
Hand sanitiser feels cold as it evaporates,
and the Sun's heat evaporates seawater in salt ponds.
A class measured the final temperature for four changes.
Every one started at 20 degrees Celsius.
Dissolving calcium chloride ended at 38 degrees,
and neutralising an acid with an alkali at 27.
But the drink with melting ice fell to 8 degrees,
and dissolving ammonium chloride fell to 12.
Pause and decide: which of these four changes are exothermic,
and which are endothermic?
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: A reaction makes a test tube feel warm.
Is it exothermic or endothermic?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Exothermic – it releases heat.
Question 2: Is freezing exothermic or endothermic?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Exothermic – heat is released as water turns to ice.
Question 3: Give one example of an endothermic reaction.
Pause the video now.
Answer: e.g. photosynthesis, thermal decomposition, citric acid + baking soda.
Question 4: Why does hand sanitiser make your hands feel cold?
Pause the video now.
Answer: It evaporates, taking in heat from your skin.

rubric.pt: Pattern: more mass gives a bigger fall (about 3 °C per gram)
The 4 g result (6.1 °C) is anomalous

adv.model: As the mass of sodium hydrogencarbonate increases, the temperature fall gets bigger, by about 3 °C for each gram. The result for 4 g is anomalous because the fall is only 6.1 °C. Following the pattern it should be about 12 °C, so this test should be repeated. The temperature falls because the reaction is endothermic. It takes in energy from the water in the solution, so the solution gets colder.

partial.text: The temperature goes down every time some powder is added to the acid. This is because the reaction takes in energy when it happens. It is a chemical reaction because a gas is made and it fizzes. The student measured the temperature with a thermometer.

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A dry thermometer reads 20.0 °C. A thermometer with a wet cloth around its bulb reads 17.5 °C in still air, and 14.0 °C when a fan blows on it. Use the particle model to explain both results.
adv.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: Water evaporates from the wet cloth
Evaporation is endothermic: it takes in energy from the thermometer
The particles with the most energy escape, leaving slower ones
The fan moves air / vapour away, so evaporation is faster
Uses data: falls of 2.5 °C and 6.0 °C

adv.model: Water evaporates from the wet cloth around the bulb. Evaporation is endothermic, so it takes in energy from the thermometer. The particles with the most energy escape from the liquid, leaving slower particles behind, so the reading falls by 2.5 °C. With the fan, moving air carries the water vapour away, so evaporation happens faster. More energy is taken in each minute, so the reading falls further, by 6.0 °C.

partial.text: The water in the cloth evaporates and this makes the thermometer colder. That is why it shows 17.5 °C instead of 20.0 °C. The fan makes it even colder, 14.0 °C, because it blows cold air onto the bulb. So the wet thermometer with the fan is the coldest one.
partial.why: Evaporation and data; the fan idea is wrong (the air is not colder) and there is no particle idea

partial.text: Evaporation takes in energy, so the wet thermometer is colder than the dry one. The water on the cloth slowly turns into a gas in the air. The fan makes the water evaporate faster, so the reading is the coldest of all. This is like when you feel cold after swimming.
partial.why: Energy, evaporation and the fan; no particle model and no data

adv.prompt: * Advanced. A student says: 'Dissolving ammonium chloride made the water cold, so it must be a chemical reaction.' Evaluate this claim.

rubric.pt: a temperature change alone does not prove a chemical reaction
dissolving / melting are physical changes that can be endothermic
evidence of a reaction needs a new substance (e.g. gas, precipitate)

adv.model: The claim is wrong. Physical changes such as dissolving and melting can also take in or give out heat. Dissolving ammonium chloride is an endothermic physical process: no new substance is made, so a temperature change on its own does not prove a chemical reaction.

ext.prompt: A student says: “Photosynthesis is endothermic, so a greenhouse full of plants should be colder than an empty greenhouse.” Evaluate this claim.
ext.frame: The data show … For example, at … the value was … This is because … The results are / are not reliable because …

rubric.pt: Photosynthesis takes in energy from light
The energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose
The energy comes from light, not from the thermal energy of the air, so it does not cool the greenhouse
kw: not from the (air|surroundings|thermal)|does not cool|doesn.t cool|not colder

rubric.pt: Plants also respire, which is exothermic
Conclusion: the claim is not supported (any cooling would be from evaporation or shade)

ext.model: Photosynthesis is endothermic because plants take in energy from light. This energy is stored as chemical energy in glucose. However, the energy comes from light, not from the thermal energy of the air, so photosynthesis does not cool the greenhouse. Plants also respire, which is exothermic and releases some energy. Water evaporating from the leaves could cool the air a little, but that is not caused by photosynthesis, so the claim is not supported.

partial.text: I agree with the student because photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction. Endothermic reactions take in heat from the surroundings. So the plants take heat from the air in the greenhouse. This means a greenhouse full of plants would be colder than an empty one.
partial.why: Confuses energy from light with thermal energy from the air

partial.text: Photosynthesis uses light energy from the Sun to make glucose. The energy is stored in the glucose as chemical energy. Plants also respire all the time and respiration gives out energy. So I do not think the greenhouse with plants would be colder, and the claim is wrong.
partial.why: Light, glucose, respiration and a conclusion; does not explain why light energy does not cool the air

ext.prompt: Thermal decomposition of 2.0 g of copper carbonate takes in 1.8 kJ of energy. How much energy is needed to decompose 5.0 g?
ext.hint: Find the energy for 1 g first.
ext.reason: 1.8 kJ ÷ 2.0 g = 0.9 kJ per gram, so 5.0 g needs 0.9 × 5.0 = 4.5 kJ.

ext.model: For the cold pack I would use ammonium nitrate, because it gives the biggest fall of 9.5 °C. Dissolving it is endothermic, so it takes in energy from the surroundings. For the hot pack I would use calcium chloride, because its temperature rises by 12.0 °C. Dissolving calcium chloride is exothermic, so it releases energy. Sodium chloride is no use for either pack because its change of 0.5 °C is too small. Each salt was tested only once, so the tests should be repeated with the same mass and volume of water.

partial.text: I would use ammonium nitrate for the cold pack and calcium chloride for the hot pack. This is because they change the temperature the most of all the salts.
